episodes.193221: Training thunderstorms moved through Central Sumter County on the evening of August 12th producing up to 3.5 inches of rain in a few hours resulting in areas of localized flooding.
episodes.193222: The combination of an upper trough and a passing shortwave along with 750-1500 J/kg of surface based CAPE and bulk shear of 25-35 knots promoted the development of scattered thunderstorms, a few of which became strong to severe.
episodes.193273: A mesoscale convective complex developed over Kansas during the early morning of August 13, 2024 and continued east towards southwest Missouri during the remainder of the morning. Despite the progressive nature of the system, heavy rainfall between 2 and 4.40 inches fell over Greene, Vernon, and Dade counties.
episodes.193995: Slow moving thunderstorms produced flash flooding with up to four inches of rainfall reported in Brush and north of Punkin Center. In addition to the heavy rainfall, hail up to two inches in diameter and 68 mph winds were reported.
episodes.194003: Thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado August 13th producing strong to damaging winds. A wind gust of 83 mph was reported was four miles north-northeast of Elizabeth. The strongest wind gust of the day. The Fire department reported a collapsed outbuilding due to wind damage near intersection of Private Road 160 and County Road 21 near where the 83 mph wind gust was reported.
episodes.194232: Multiple, slow moving storms trained across portions of east central Kansas during the morning hours, resulting in the highest rainfall amounts from 4 to 6 inches. This caused flash flooding in the Emporia area.
episodes.195094: A thunderstorm passed over the Riverton airport and produced a wind gust of 60 mph.
episodes.195434: A complex of thunderstorms moved eastward into portions of central and south central Kansas during the early morning hours of August 13th. These storms began to pick up some steam as they approached the Interstate 135 corridor, and they started producing 55 to 60 mph wind gusts between Newton and Wichita. Fortunately, little damage was reported.
episodes.195457: A Mesoscale Convective System developed in eastern Oklahoma and northwestern Arkansas in the early morning hours of August 12th. This MCS was fairly short-lived, decaying by that evening over north-central Mississippi. The residual boundary slowly sagged south through the day on August 13th. It reached the Mississippi coast during peak heating and provided sufficient lift to support intensifying thunderstorms. Those storms produced severe wind gusts at multiple marine observation locations along the Mississippi coast and the Mississippi Sound.
episodes.195760: The combination of daytime heating/destabilization and weak winds near a surface boundary lingering across the Charleston County coast led to thunderstorms capable of producing waterspouts.
episodes.195898: Torrential downpours with between two and five inches of rain moved through the Bismarck area as a very slow moving thunderstorm passed over. Storm sewer and drainage systems in the city were overwhelmed by the intense rain rates. Many downtown businesses took on water, resulting in damaged inventory along with business losses due to inaccessibility and time taken to recover. One of the primary medical centers in the downtown area had up to two inches of flooding on the main floor, which caused damage to the lower level, particularly to an MRI machine. This facility alone suffered damages in excess of 5 million dollars, primarily due to the damage caused to the MRI machine. The City of Bismarck government services suffered approximately a quarter-million dollars in damage, which included damage to property, infrastructure, and equipment. Many homes also sustained water damage, particularly in basements. One homeowner near the Elks swimming pool, which is just west of downtown, reported up to five feet of water in his basement. An apartment complex in central Bismarck had three feet of water in the lower level, with occupants having to evacuate for multiple days. Interestingly, just south of Bismarck, in Falconer Estates, there was a trace of rain.
episodes.195958: Strong thunderstorms moved across the marine area and produced gusty winds.
episodes.195975: A weak front dropped south into the combined Panhandles and stalled across the region on August 12th. A combination of daytime heating, adequate instability and wind shear allowed for a few storms to become strong to severe and produce severe hail.
episodes.196072: Monsoonal showers and thunderstorms brought flash flooding and gusty winds to Utah.
episodes.196073: With a mid-level monsoonal moisture plume already in place, and a passing shortwave trough in the upper levels, a few strong to severe storms developed over portions of the plains from the 12th thru 13th of August, and also resulted in some heavy amounts of rain over El Paso County. A wet microburst from a thunderstorm also produced wind damage around the city of Pueblo due to brief gusty winds being greater than hurricane force.
episodes.196083: Ample monoon moisture and slow moving thunderstorms brought lightning, heavy rain, and flash flooding to a few locations across northern Arizona.
episodes.196084: Monsoon moisture over northern Arizona and Utah brought showers and thunderstorms to those areas. This caused several spikes to the Paria River at the confluence of the Colorado River.  There also were several spikes in the flow in the days before this episode.
episodes.196089: Several reports of severe weather received.
episodes.196158: Lightning sparked a small house fire in Clarkston.
episodes.196236: An isolated waterspout developed over the Gulf of Mexico waters near Sugarloaf Key.  A light southeast wind flow was present along with residual Saharan Air Layer detected by the Key West morning sounding.

Heavy rain over far northern Arizona and south-central Utah caused several spikes on the Paria River just before it joined the Colorado River upstream from The Grand Canyon. The water flow started to increase (from 4.98 feet) around 100 PM MST on August 13.  There were three crests in the flow: 6.24 feet at 500 PM, 704 feet at 800 PM MST on August 13, and 7.66 feet at 300 AM MST on August 14. The flow returned to near normal at around 1100 PM on August 14.
